title: MB1-01279
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: Respondents XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are citizens of Romania. They obtained refugee status in Canada on September 21, 2005. The Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness (hereinafter referred to as the Minister) is applying to the panel to determine that the respondents' refugee protection has ceased because the respondents voluntarily re-availed themselves of the protection of their country of nationality.

The mother, XXXX XXXX, acted as the designated representative for XXXX XXXX, who was 17 years of age on the day of the hearing. The mother was designated as such during the proceedings in respect of the refugee protection claim as well as for all subsequent proceedings before the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB), as stipulated in subrule 20(6) of the Rules.

The respondents claimed refugee protection using a Personal Information Form (hereinafter referred to as the PIF), which they submitted to the IRB on May 13, 2005, and August 9, 2005. In their PIF, the respondents allege that they are victims of persecution in their country of origin by reason of their Roma nationality.
Their hearing before the IRB was held on September 7, 2005. On September 21, 2005, the IRB granted them refugee protection and established their status as Convention refugees.

On April 14, 2010, the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) made a mail seizure and found the passports of the five respondents: Romanian passports issued on XXXX XXXX, 2008, for XXXX, on XXXX XXXX, 2008, for XXXX, on XXXX XXXX, 2008, for XXXX XXXX and on XXXX XXXX, 2008, for XXXX and XXXX. These passports were issued in Romania by means of a power of attorney signed by the respondents.
None of the respondents have permanent residence in Canada yet.

Taking into account all the evidence on record, the panel determines that the respondents' refugee protection has ceased because they voluntarily re-availed themselves of the protection of their country of nationality, Romania. ANALYSIS Steps taken to reach the respondents who did not attend the hearing

On February 23, 2011, the Minister sent the respondents the notice of intervention for this hearing. The IRB received a copy of this notice on February 25, 2011. On March 4, 2011, the panel sent the respondents a letter asking them for the name of their counsel. The panel's mail was returned on two occasions, on March 17, 2011, and March 23, 2011. The mail was sent to two different addresses.

The panel sent a notice to appear, on February 23, 2012, the mail was returned. After receiving a new address found by the CBSA, on March 7, 2012, the panel sent another notice to appear on March 13, 2013. On March 22, 2012, the panel received a request for postponement from a counsel with respect to the hearing set for April 12, 2012. The request was granted. A new hearing date was scheduled for November 12, 2013. On October 29, 2013, a new counsel requested a postponement of the scheduled hearing. That request was granted. The hearing was scheduled for January 10, 2014.

On the day of the hearing, some of the respondents attended, namely, XXXX, XXXX and XXXX. The counsel attended, but he requested a postponement because he was XXXX. The postponement was granted because of the counsel's XXXX XXXX. The panel asked the attending respondents where XXXX and XXXX XXXX were. XXXX stated that they were in Vancouver. The panel explained to the principal respondent that they would have to attend the next hearing, to be held on March 25, 2014. The panel gave them sufficient time to take the steps required to be able to attend in Montréal. At the March 25, 2014, hearing the panel noted that XXXX and XXXX XXXX were absent again. They did not request that the panel postpone the hearing or change the location or that they be heard by other means. As a result, the panel nevertheless proceeded with the hearing in the absence of those two respondents. In addition, the mother stated that she had sent them to Ireland and that she would look after their interests. Furthermore, the counsel in attendance was representing them. Cessation of refugee protection

In light of the evidence, the Minister is applying to the panel to determine that the respondents' refugee protection has ceased because they voluntarily re-availed themselves of the protection of their country of nationality, Romania, pursuant to paragraph 108(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

The panel will refer to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees Handbook for assistance in deciding this application; articles 118 to 125 deal with this clause. The clause implies three requirements to apply: the refugee must act voluntarily, he must intend by his action to re-avail himself of the protection of the country of his nationality, and he must actually obtain such protection. In addition, according to article 121 of the Handbook: If a refugee applies for and obtains a national passport or its renewal, it will, in the absence of proof to the contrary, be presumed that he intends to avail himself of the protection of the country of his nationality.

The respondents allegedly obtained a Romanian passport issued in Romania on different dates, as stated in the allegations. The respondents indicated through counsel in Exhibit M-7 that they applied for these passports to make it easier for them to travel to Ireland because, based on their explanations, travelling with a refugee travel document is complicated, as getting to Ireland directly is often difficult. Their Romanian passport makes it easier for them to travel.

At the hearing, the respondents acknowledged that they applied for and obtained Romanian passports. The principal respondent explained that she applied for them during a trip to Ireland, the exact date of which she could no longer recall. She and her children-XXXX XXXX, XXXX (born in 1997) and XXXX-allegedly left Canada with a refugee travel document. They transited through Germany and, upon their arrival there, it was impossible for them to get to Ireland. At that point, she allegedly contacted a cousin in Romania and sent him a power of attorney so that he could obtain Romanian passports for her and her accompanying children, namely, XXXX XXXX, XXXX (born in 1997) and XXXX. They allegedly used them only to go to Ireland. She and her children allegedly left with their refugee travel documents and forgot all their Romanian passports in Ireland. The documents allegedly remained there in the principal respondent's purse. However, XXXX travelled to Ireland later, and the principal respondent took the same steps to obtain a passport for him.

With respect to the respondent's willingness, the panel is of the opinion that they obtained their passports voluntarily. The respondents were not forced to do so. They did so of their own accord in order to travel to Ireland more quickly and more easily.

With respect to intention, the respondents alleged that they applied for their passports to make it easier for them to travel to Ireland. However, the panel notes that they chose to travel using a Romanian passport rather than their refugee travel document accompanied by the appropriate visa. In fact, they travelled to Germany using a refugee travel document, subsequently applied for a Romanian passport to get to Ireland, and left Ireland for Canada using their refugee travel documents. The respondents were in no way obliged to use a Romanian passport to get to Ireland. They could have taken steps and obtained the visas required for their trip from Canadian authorities. The panel does not believe that the respondents did not know that they were unable to travel to Europe other than with their Romanian passport, since the principal respondent started her trip using the refugee travel document and, moreover, the principal respondent acknowledged at the hearing that the two children who were not at the hearing were in Ireland at that time and that they had again travelled using their Romanian passports. This is so, despite the fact that they knew that the Minister had initiated proceedings against them. The panel also does not believe that the respondents forgot their Romanian passports in Ireland, because the respondents did not all travel together. XXXX returned to Canada from Ireland on XXXX XXXX, 2014. He left his passport in Ireland while the other respondents were still there. XXXX explained that, when she had travelled with XXXX, XXXX and XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX, she forgot the passports in Ireland. If the respondents had truly forgotten them, they would have asked a family member in Ireland to send them as quickly as possible. Instead, the passports were sent in XXXX 2010, nearly two years later. That is when the CBSA made the mail seizure. The panel is of the opinion that the respondents wanted to hide from Canadian authorities the fact that they had applied for Romanian passports.

Given the lack of credibility and despite the fact that the respondents alleged that they did not travel to Romania using their Romanian passports, the panel is of the opinion that, on a balance of probabilities, the respondents' intention was to go to Romania, as the only reason for obtaining the passport was the fact that a refugee travel document allows an individual to travel anywhere, except to their country of persecution, in this case, Romania.
The fact that they procured passports is evidence that they obtained protection. The passports for which they applied were issued to them.

For the above-mentioned reasons, the panel is of the opinion that the respondents failed to rebut the presumption that they wanted to re-avail themselves of the protection of their country of nationality by obtaining the passports. This also applies to the two respondents who did not attend the hearing, namely, XXXX and XXXX XXXX. They were minors when their passports were issued in 2008. However, it was not shown that their intention at that time was different from the intention of their mother, the principal respondent.
The panel finds that the Minister discharged his burden of proof and that the respondents voluntarily re-availed themselves of the protection of their country of citizenship, Romania.

After analyzing all the evidence, the panel allows the application to cease refugee protection filed by the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness. The panel determines that the refugee protection of the respondents has ceased pursuant to subsection 108(2) of the IRPA.

The refugee protection claims of XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX must therefore be rejected. The respondents are neither "Convention refugees" nor "persons in need of protection" because they voluntarily re-availed themselves of the protection of their country of nationality, Romania. Linda Doutre Linda Doutre June 2, 2014 Date IRB translation Original language: French RPD File No. / No de dossier de la SPR : MB1-01279 1
